sources.citation: Crump, Des. 2020. Language of the Week: Week Three - Dalleburra. State Library of Queensland blog, 15 June 2020.
sources.note: Nothing on phonology or stress. A short library blog post: 'Robert Christison, who took up Lammermoor Station in 1863 documented language and culture of the local Dalleburra people.. The State Library holds the Christison Family Papers and Lammermoor Station Records [TR1867].. Within the papers are several wordlists which were later used as source materials for publications, including Breen, Tindale and Curr. Mary Montgomerie Bennett, Christison's daughter, also published an English-Dalleburra wordlist in Christison of Lammermoor'. Mentions revival support by the North Queensland Regional Abo…
sources.venue: State Library of Queensland blog, 15 June 2020

sources.citation: Crump, Desmond. 2019. 2019 International Year of Indigenous Languages: Word of the Week - Week Fourteen [Yirandali 'woodoobra']. State Library of Queensland blog, 2 April 2019.
sources.note: No phonology content. One word ('woodoobra', 'lotus flower', from Christison's 1860s Lammermoor wordlist via Bennett 1927 'Dalleburra additional words'), a note that Yirandali 'is undergoing an active community language revival' supported by the North Queensland Regional Aboriginal Corporation Language Centre, and a source list (TR1867 Christison Family Papers; Bennett 1927 JRAI 57; further reading Bailey 1909, Brayshaw 1990, Breen 1990, Curr 1887, Tindale 1974).
sources.venue: State Library of Queensland blog, 2 April 2019

sources.citation: Bowern, Claire (comp.). Pama-Nyungan lexical database (lexibank 'bowernpny' CLDF, from Bowern & Atkinson 2012), language 'Yirandali' (145 forms, source Bowern2012).
sources.note: Wordlist only: 145 items in 19th-century English-based spelling with automatic segmentation; no stress or pitch marks; no statement.

sources.citation: Breen, Gavan. 2009. The Biri dialects and their neighbours. Transactions of the Royal Society of South Australia 133(2): 219-256.
sources.note: Only modern linguist's treatment that covers Yirandhali (as a neighbour of Biri); the one Glottolog 'overview' ref. Abstract indicates a source/territory review rather than phonology, but if Breen anywhere comments on Yirandhali forms (e.g. from Tindale's stress-marked transcriptions) it would be here.
sources.venue: Transactions of the Royal Society of South Australia

sources.citation: Breen, Gavan. 1990. Salvage studies of western Queensland Aboriginal languages. Pacific Linguistics B-105. Canberra: ANU. (pp.5, 66-67, 118 and references; full text already held by the project at
sources.note: Nothing on Yirandhali stress. Lists all Yirandhali sources (Armstrong 1886, Christison 1887, M. & E. Curr 1886, Dalhunty 1887, I.S. Dutton 1906, Tindale 1938-39 MS, Anonymous 1900 -- all wordlists) and explicitly leaves 'a study of Yirandhali' to 'a later time (and, I hope, another person)' (p.67). Yirandhali not among the languages described.

sources.citation: Bennett, M. M. 1927. Notes on the Dalleburra tribe of northern Queensland. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland 57: 399-415, pls. doi:10.2307/2843711.
sources.note: No phonology content. Ethnographic account from Robert Christison's notes; a few cited words (mung-er 'to hear', koolbinny 'throwing-stick', mambo 'corroboree'), remarks that the people conversed fluently in Dalleburra and learned English quickly, and Appendix B, a list of c.15 words 'additional to the Dalleburra dictionary published in E. M. Curr's The Australian Race'. No accent marks, no remark on pronunciation or stress.
sources.venue: Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland

sources.citation: Palmer, Edward. 1883 [publ. 1884]. Notes on some Australian tribes (with an Appendix of Aboriginal words, pp.326-334, and Appendix II, Remarks on Mr. Palmer's class systems by A. W. Howitt, pp.335-347). Journal of the Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland 13: 276-347. doi:10.2307/2841896.
sources.note: No prosodic content. The 'Languages' section (pp.307-310) has only general remarks: shared words across the continent, 'white men do not always catch the sounds.. T becomes th, or d, and the sound ng often becomes k', tooth avulsion affecting pronunciation; verb paradigms are Mycoolon. Any Yerrunthully words are confined to the appendix table (wordlist only, no accent marks visible in scanned).
sources.venue: Journal of the Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland
